cards.text: Nahum the prophet has already said it: the LORD will make an end of Nineveh. Now one who scatters is marching on the city, and friend, that is NOT who you want showing up on the doorbell camera. Nahum calls out, "Guard the fortress! Watch the road! Brace yourselves! Summon all your strength!"

cards.question: In the middle of all that, Nahum turns to Jacob. Destroyers laid Jacob waste and ruined the branches of their vine. What will the LORD do for Jacob?

cards.text: The attackers roll in with red shields, warriors dressed in scarlet, and chariot fittings that flash like fire. Friend, I can't even match my apron to my hat, and these folks COORDINATED.

cards.question: The chariots dash through the streets and rush around the plazas. What does Nahum say they look like?

cards.text: Someone summons his nobles, and they stumble as they advance, like me carrying a full tray to the oven. They race to the wall, and the protective shield is set in place.

cards.question: The river gates are thrown open, but the palace stands firm.
With the palace down, what is decreed for the city?

answers.text: That it be exiled and carried away
That it pay a yearly tribute
That it be rebuilt in stone

cards.text: Listen to that. Her maidservants moan like doves and beat upon their breasts.
Then Nahum paints a picture. All her days, Nineveh has been like a pool of water.

cards.question: Nineveh has been like a pool of water all her days. What is happening to that pool now?
As the pool drains, the cry goes out, "Stop! Stop!" and no one turns back.

cards.text: Then a new shout goes up: "Plunder the silver! Plunder the gold!" Friend, that's not a battle cry anymore. That's the doors opening on Black Friday.

cards.question: Once the plundering starts, Nineveh's treasure runs out fast.
After the plundering, how does Nahum describe Nineveh?
As Nineveh is emptied, Nahum says knees knock and every face grows pale.

cards.text: Then Nahum asks a question. Where is the lions' lair now, the feeding ground where the lion and lioness prowled with nothing to frighten them away?

cards.question: In Nahum's picture, the lion mauled enough for its ___ and filled its dens with ___.
Then the LORD of Hosts speaks. He declares that He is ___ you.

cards.text: And He spells it out. He'll reduce the chariots to cinders, the sword will devour the young lions, and He'll cut off the prey from the earth.

cards.question: One more thing the LORD says will be gone. What will no longer be heard?

findings.problem: The opening card runs past 3 sentences. It has three sentences of its own, then quotes all four commands from Nahum 2:1, for seven sentences in total.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on.

findings.problem: Jacob appears for the first time, and the card never says who he is (God's people, Israel). The card also says Nahum 'turns to Jacob', which makes Jacob the one being spoken to. Nahum 2:2 only says the LORD will restore Jacob's splendor. It does not address Jacob.

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: 'Nahum turns to Jacob' says who is being addressed, but the text leaves that open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The question asks what the chariots 'look like', and the answer is 'Torches and lightning'. In Nahum 2:4 only the torches are about how they look ('appearing like torches'). The lightning is about how they move ('darting about like lightning').
This story card is a flat retelling with no Papa Dorin voice or humor.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: This story card is a flat setup with no Papa Dorin voice. Card 10's question then repeats its whole content.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The answer depends on how the baker reads the statement. 'Nineveh's treasure runs out fast' is marked False because of 2:9 ('There is no end to the treasure'). But 2:10 says 'She is emptied!', so a baker could argue it's True. Card 12's Black Friday joke, with its picture of shelves being stripped, also pushes the baker toward True.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: This story card is a flat retelling of 2:11 with no Papa Dorin voice or humor.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The question says 'He is ___ you' and never says who 'you' is (Nineveh, named in 2:1 and 2:8). The baker can't see the earlier cards, and could read 'you' as themselves.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: This story card is a flat list of the LORD's words with almost no Papa Dorin voice.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: Across the stop, only cards 1, 3, 5 and 12 carry a joke. The other four story cards read as plain narration, so the stop is mildly pleasant rather than funny.

rule.text: But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
